title: Goal
text: Drifter, level 0 - a Vortex-style remote syscall service. We ssh in as drifter0 on port 2230; the source of /drifter/drifter0 and its two C files are world-readable. The daemon chroots to /home/drifter0/chroot where drifter0.password sits (33 bytes, mode 400), drops to uid 19000, listens on localhost:1111, and executes arbitrary i386 syscalls that arrive in RC4-encrypted 36-byte frames. The syscall interface is the whole game.

title: The protocol: RC4 keyed by how the server sees us
text: Reading the source: every frame is 9 dwords (syscall number plus 8 arguments), RC4-encrypted with a keystream whose key material is the 4-byte source IP plus the 2-byte source port AS THE SERVER SEES THEM - getpeername on the daemon side. The RC4 state persists across frames in both directions, so the client must mirror the server's state machine exactly: one stream for requests, one for replies. The catch: behind NAT you can't know your server-visible port. But the cast runs on the shared backend, where the daemon sees 127.0.0.1 and the client's own ephemeral port - which getsockname() on the client socket reports exactly.

title: The client: mirror the state machine, call syscalls
text: drifter0_client.py (typed in vi) implements prepare_key over the 6-byte keymat and the rc4() stepper, then call(): encrypt the 9-dword frame, send it, recv 4 bytes, decrypt with the reply state. The run prints the resolved keymat - 7f000001 plus the ephemeral port in hex - then drives three syscalls: open the password file (fd 3), read 33 bytes ('read file -> 33'), and write them back over the reply channel - the EXFIL line prints the raw bytes: yttCfzKiorcOz5V0Nr9AVk6SZ13IonYV.

title: Verify
text: cat /home/drifter0/chroot/drifter0.password shows the same string the syscall service exfiltrated. The password is the account's own - the verification IS the login. Drifter 0 done.
